chapters.title: What Is Radio? (And Why Zombies Should Care)
chapters.html:
Welcome, post-civ survivor! Whether you're scavenging K-pop t-shirts or building a bunker out of PlayStation cases, you’ll soon discover that radio is the real cheat-code for communication in the end times.

What Counts as "Radio"?

  • Radio is electromagnetic energy, part of the spectrum squeezed between sound waves and microwaves.
  • It’s how walkie-talkies, satellites, airport scanners, your Bluetooth speaker, and even some microwaves talk to each other.
  • Radios work by tossing electromagnetic waves (oscillating electric and magnetic fields) through space at the speed of light.
  • Radio = electric and magnetic fields oscillating together
  • Frequency (f), wavelength (λ), and the speed of light (c) are related by λ = cf.
  • Radio is strictly physical, not magic — and sometimes, not even digital!

A Brief Meme-Ridden History of Radio

  • In the 1930s-1940s, radios were living room centerpieces, bigger than most survivors' bugout bags.
  • Orson Welles panicked a nation with La Guerra de los Mundos (War of the Worlds) — proving radios could out-troll TikTok, even before trolls existed.
  • Old-time shows were like audio Netflix, with suspense, laughs, and science fiction all at the twist of a dial.

Why Bother After the End of the World?

  • When the grid dies and cell towers are overrun by zombies (or just out-of-service teens), only radio still connects people.
  • All modern “wireless” stuff — WiFi, Bluetooth, walkie-talkies, GPS, remote car keys, contactless credit cards — is just radio in a fancier wrapper.
  • True apocalypse survivors use radio for:
    • Long-distance memes and squad comms.
    • Weather alerts (to avoid mutant hurricanes).
    • Fox hunting (actually finding hidden transmissions, not animals).
    • Disaster coordination and hacking.
    • Trolling and eavesdropping on the unprepared.

Key Radio Terms You Actually Need

Term Meaning Example & Meme
Frequency (f) Swings per second (Hertz, Hz) 100 MHz = FM radio
Wavelength (λ) Distance between cycle peaks (c/f), usually in meters 3 meters for 100 MHz
Modulation Encoding information on a wave AM, FM, FSK, PSK, all the classics
Bandwidth How much information you can pack into a signal Narrowband walkie-talkie vs. Netflix stream
Spectrum The whole range of radio frequencies "The wild west of waves"

Next Up

  • The nuts and bolts: what makes “waves” work, what’s really inside a radio, and how to spot signals in the wild like a true radio witcher.

chapters.title: The Physics of Waves — How Radio Becomes Superpowered
chapters.html:
Introduction: Why Physics Matters (Even in the Zombie Apocalypse)

Before you start building antennas, hacking signals, or jammin’ droids, you gotta understand what actually makes a radio wave. Think of radio not as magic but as pure electromagnetic (EM) energy traveling at light-speed in the chaos of the spectrum.

Electromagnetic Waves: The Core Concept

  • All radio signals are EM waves, oscillating electric (E) and magnetic (B) fields intertwined.
  • These waves are transverse, meaning the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to the wave’s direction.
  • They carry energy across space, bouncing around like the chaos in a zombie horde.

Wave Parameters: Wavelength, Frequency, Speed

Speed of Light

  • All EM waves travel at c = 299,792,458  m/s.
  • Imagine them as zombies moving at the speed of light—nothing can outrun them.

Wavelength (λ)

  • Distance between two wave peaks.
  • λ = cf, where f is the frequency.

Frequency (f)

  • How many wave peaks pass a point per second.
  • Hz (Hertz) for normal radios, kHz, MHz, GHz for different piles of spectrum.

Example Calculation

  • A 100 MHz FM station has a wavelength:
    λ = 3 × 108108 = 3  m.

How Waves Propagate

Line of Sight (LOS)

  • In open terrain, waves travel straight like a laser beam—perfect for clear radio paths.
  • No hills or zombies in the way: simple, direct.

Reflection & Diffraction

  • When disruptive terrain (buildings, mountains, zombies) are present, waves bounce or bend.
  • Critical for communication across ruins: antennas and waveguides are modern-day magic tools.

Interference & Multipath

  • Multiple waves colliding may cancel out or amplify each other.
  • Your signal could be zombie-strong or zombie-weak, depending on the chaos.

Attenuation & Signal Loss

  • As waves travel, they weaken — similar to a meme losing punch the further it spreads.
  • Decibels (dB) measure how much the signal drops.
  • dB = 10 × log10(PoutPin)

Modulation & Data Embedding

  • Embedding info onto waves—like surreptitious radio memes or encrypted alien transmissions.
  • Types:
    • Amplitude Modulation (AM): Change the wave’s volume.
    • Frequency Modulation (FM): Change the pitch.
    • Phase Shift Keying (PSK): Shift the wave’s phase—great for hackers.
    • Frequency-Shift Keying (FSK): Switch between different frequencies.

Signal Spectrum: The Wild West

  • Different signals occupy different bands:
    • ELF (Extremely Low Frequency): Deep underground comms.
    • VLF (Very Low Frequency): Submarine comms.
    • HF (High Frequency, 3-30 MHz): CB, shortwave, pirate radio.
    • VHF, UHF (Very/Ultra High Frequency): TV, FM, cell phones, WiFi.
    • Microwaves (GHz): Radar, satellite links, microwave ovens.

How to Visualize EM Waves

  • Imagine a wave as a roller coaster: height = electric field, vertical length = magnetic field.

  • Wavelength is the distance from the hilltops, frequency is how often the roller coaster rides pass.

  • Propagation techniques

  • Wave polarization and antenna interaction

  • Signal strength and difficult terrain

  • Building your first simple antenna

Keep this as your mental toolkit: understanding the waves makes hacking, building, or surviving with radios possible even when the zombies are knocking on your door.

chapters.title: Signal Science — Types, Strength, and Survival
chapters.html:
Overview: Why Signal Matters in Apocalypse Radio

If you want reliable comms, hack the spectrum, or just yak with your crew while zombies roam, understanding signal types, behaviors, and strengths is a must. This chapter unlocks the physics, math, and practicalities of signals—your lifeline in the airwaves.

Signal Types and Modulations

  • Continuous Wave (CW): Simple on/off pulses, Morse code style, zombie classic.
  • Amplitude Modulation (AM): Vary signal strength to encode info; simple but noise-prone.
  • Frequency Modulation (FM): Shift frequency; less noise, better music and voices.
  • Phase Shift Keying (PSK): Hack-level encoding by changing phase of wave.
  • Frequency Shift Keying (FSK): Digital style frequency switches.
  • Spread Spectrum: Secret sauce for jam resistance and secure comms (includes FHSS and DSSS).

Signal Strength & Measuring Power

  • Signal power measured in Watts (W) or dBm (decibels referenced to 1 milliwatt).
  • P(dBm) = 10 × log10 left(P(W)1mWright).
  • Field strength (Volts per meter, V/m) tells actual wave voltage in air.
  • Free space path loss (FSPL) law describes how signal weakens with distance d:

FSPL(dB) = 20 log10(d) + 20 log10(f) + 20 log10 left(4πcright)

  • Practical survival tip: antenna gain can boost received signal strength by degrees.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)

  • How clean your signal is vs background noise.
  • High SNR = clear messages; low SNR = zombie static and confusion.
  • Techniques to improve SNR:
    • Use directional antennas.
    • Increase transmitter power or receiver sensitivity.
    • Use digital protocols with error correction.

Doppler Effect in Radio

  • Moving zombies and vehicles change perceived frequency.
  • Important for fast-moving drones or when tracking survivors.
  • Formula for shifted frequency:

f' = f × c + vrc + vs

where vr and vs are velocities of receiver and source.

Advanced Signal Handling

  • Filtering: Removing unwanted frequencies/noise.
  • Mixing and Heterodyning: Creating new frequencies by combining signals.
  • IQ Modulation: Complex amplitude and phase control for SDR and advanced radios.

Signal Types Summary Table

Signal Type Characteristics Usage Apocalypse Utility
CW (Morse Code) Simple on/off Basic text messaging Stealth comms with minimal power
AM Strength varies, noisier AM radio, simple voice Low-tech, widely understood
FM Frequency varies, noise-resistant Radio broadcasting Clearer voice, music transmission
PSK, FSK Digital phase/freq modulation Data comms, hacking Secure, efficient data transfer
Spread Spectrum Hopping/fading frequencies Military, secure radio Resistant to jamming, secure ops

chapters.title: Antennas — Your Signal’s Best Friend (and Sometimes Worst Enemy)
chapters.html:
Why Antennas Are the Game-Changers

No matter how powerful your transmitter or clever your code, an antenna is what throws your message into the wild and catches the buzz from your squad. Knowing antennas means knowing how to maximize range, minimize noise, and survive the signal jungle.

Antenna Basics

  • An antenna converts electric signals into EM waves for transmission and vice versa for reception.
  • It behaves as an electrical conductor matched to a wavelength or fraction thereof.
  • Types include dipoles, loops, yagis, ground planes, and fractals.
  • Resonance: Antennas must be tuned to their operational frequency for maximum efficiency.
  • Polarization: Vertical, horizontal, or circular polarization affect signal clarity and range.

Antenna Theory Highlights

Radiation Pattern

  • Describes how an antenna distributes energy in space.
  • Omni-directional antennas radiate equally in all directions.
  • Directional antennas focus energy in specific directions for longer range or less interference.

Gain

  • Measures antenna efficiency and focus compared to a theoretical isotropic radiator.
  • Expressed in dBi (decibels over isotropic radiator).
  • Higher gain = longer directed reach but narrower beamwidth.

Bandwidth

  • Frequency range over which the antenna operates effectively.
  • Wider bandwidth helps handle signal hopping and multipath fading.

Practical Antenna Tips For Survivors

  • Use the longest wire possible for simple dipoles.
  • Raise your antenna away from metallic surfaces to avoid signal loss.
  • Ground planes and radials increase effectiveness for vertical antennas.
  • Match antenna impedance (usually 50 or 75 ohms) to your radio gear to prevent reflections.

Antenna Design Formulae and Math

  • Half-wave dipole length:

L = 143fMHz meters

  • Quarter-wave vertical length:

L = 71.5fMHz meters

  • Effective radiated power (ERP) calculation:

ERP = PTx × GAnt

Diagram: Typical Dipole Antenna

Real World Antenna Projects

  • Wire dipole antenna from scavenged wire.
  • Ground plane vertical antenna using metal scraps.
  • Directional Yagi antenna for long-range zombie beaconing.

chapters.title: Radio Protocols & Data — Speaking Zombie Fluently
chapters.html:
Introduction: The Language of Radio Signals

Once you understand how radio waves travel and how antennas broadcast those waves, it's crucial to know how information is encoded and decoded. Radio protocols are the grammar and vocabulary of wireless communication — without them, your radio is just static.

Common Radio Protocols for Survivors

  • Morse Code
    Old but gold. A series of short and long signals (dots and dashes) used as a simple digital alphabet.

  • AM/FM
    Analog modulation; AM varies amplitude, FM frequency. Widely used for broadcasting voice and music.

  • Frequency Shift Keying (FSK)
    Digital method switching between frequencies to represent binary data.

  • Phase Shift Keying (PSK)
    Digital phase changes of the carrier wave. PSK31 is famous among radio hackers.

  • Packet Radio
    Transmits data in small packets with headers, checksums, and error-correction.

  • Wi-Fi & Bluetooth
    Higher-frequency protocols for local area networking and device communication.

  • LoRa / LoRaWAN
    Long-range, low-power digital modulation for IoT and survival sensor nets.

Protocol Layers Simplified

  • Physical Layer: How signals are sent (AM/FM, FSK, etc.)
  • Data Link Layer: Packet framing, error detection
  • Network Layer: Routing and addressing (mesh, IP)
  • Application Layer: Actual message content, commands.

Digital Encoding and Error Correction

  • Encoding schemes like Manchester, NRZ for reliable data recovery.
  • Error correction: Forward Error Correction (FEC), CRC codes to detect and fix errors.

Open Standards & OSS Radio Protocols

  • Popular open-source protocols you can hack on or implement for survival networks.
  • Includes APRS, AX.25, POCSAG pager codes, and much more.

Signal Timing & Synchronization

  • Clocking signals and synchronization maintain proper message decoding.
  • Important in spread-spectrum and frequency hopping protocols to avoid jamming.

Summary Table of Protocols

Protocol/Modulation Data Type Range Power Usage Typical Usage
Morse (CW) Text/Digital Long (HF/VHF) Very Low Emergency and covert comms
AM/FM Analog Voice Medium Medium Broadcasting, voice comms
FSK/PSK Digital Data Variable Medium Packet radio, data comms
Packet Radio Digital Packets Moderate Medium Amateur radio networks
Wi-Fi/Bluetooth Digital Data Short range High Local comms, IoT devices
LoRa/LoRaWAN Digital Data Very Long range Very Low Sensor networks, survive net

Introduction: Time to Get Your Hands Dirty

Theory is cool and all, but the apocalypse doesn’t care unless you turn knowledge into homebrew radios, tracking gear, or hacked comms. This chapter loads your toolkit with easy-to-follow, zombie-tested projects from hunting hidden signals to reverse engineering random remotes.

Project 1: Radio Fox Hunting — Tracking Signals Like a Zombie Pro

  • Purpose: Find hidden transmitters by triangulating their signal direction.
  • Gear: Simple directional antenna, receiver, compass, notebook.
  • Method: Walk and rotate, note signal strength and direction at various points.
  • Use triangulation math to zero in on signal origin.

Project 2: Reverse Engineering a Remote Control

  • Salvage a broken remote from the rubble.
  • Tools: Basic radio frequency receiver/debugger or SDR.
  • Decode transmitted codes by capturing signal patterns.
  • Replay hacks: replay signals with transmitter or SDR to control remote devices.

Project 3: Build Your Field Strength Meter

  • Parts: Wire loop antenna, diode (1N34A germanium recommended), analog meter.
  • Construction: Assemble as schematic to measure signal strength visually.
  • Use: Locate transmitter proximity or check antenna performance instantly.

Project 4: DIY Transmitters and Signal Boosters

  • Build a low-power AM or FM transmitter from scavenged electronics.
  • Use variable capacitors and inductors to tune frequency.
  • Safety: Always comply with legal power limits (a max 1500W transmitter project discussed later).
  • Tip: Pair transmitter with gain antennas to maximize range.

Project 5: Software Defined Radio (SDR) Basics

  • Use cheap SDR USB sticks and open-source software.
  • Receive signals from a massive range of spectrum bands.
  • Experiment with decoding paging systems, weather satellites, or emergency broadcasts.
  • Write Python scripts for automation and signal decoding.

Practical Survival Tips

  • Always carry a fiber or copper wire for impromptu antennas.
  • Have multiple hand-held scanners tuned to different bands.
  • Learn to build and test your gear from scratch to avoid zombie tech strikes.

Memory Aid: Quick Build Checklist

  • Antenna type and length ready.
  • Power source (battery, solar).
  • Receiver/transmitter assembled.
  • Test signal strength and range.
  • Log frequencies and codes.

chapters.title: Advanced Radio Hacking, Jamming, and Security — Outsmart the Horde
chapters.html:
Introduction: Going Beyond Survival

Real survivors not only build radios—they hack spectrum, defend comms, and exploit weaknesses. Welcome to the wild side where radio meets espionage, warfare, and digital trench battles.

Jamming and Anti-Jamming Tactics

  • Jamming: Intentional interference to block or confuse signals.
  • Types include barrage jamming, spot jamming, sweep jamming.
  • Anti-jamming:
    • Frequency hopping (FHSS) to jump across frequencies unpredictably.
    • Direct sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) to hide signals from interference.
    • Using directional antennas to avoid jammers.

Encryption and Secure Comms

  • Use simple ciphers (OTP, Caesar, substitution) for voice and morse.
  • Digital encryption standards in SDR and ham radio (AES, DES).
  • Steganography: embedding messages in noise or seemingly innocent data.

Protocol Hacking and Injection

  • Packet sniffing and injection for APRS, POCSAG, and pager systems.
  • Exploiting weak OTP reuse or poor key management.
  • Replay attacks: record and resend signals to gain unauthorized control.

Hardware Mods and Software Tools

  • Using SDR platforms (HackRF, RTL-SDR) to scan, decode, and inject.
  • Building jammers or spoofers from off-the-shelf parts.
  • Python and GNU Radio scripting to automate attacks or monitoring.

Ethical and Legal Warning

  • Many techniques are illegal or restricted.
  • In the apocalypse, “legal” may mean “survival,” but consequences exist.
  • Always understand your local laws and risks when experimenting.

Survival Tips

  • Keep your hackery gear hidden and mobile.
  • Use layered security in comms.
  • Stay updated on signals intelligence and jammer detection.

chapters.title: Satellite Comms, Weather, and Space Survival Radio
chapters.html:
Introduction: Beyond Earthbound — Talking Satellite and Weather Signals

When zombies crash your radio party, the sky’s the limit. Satellite and space weather radios open new doors — from tracking storms to reaching orbiting survivors.

Satellite Communications Basics

  • Satellites relay signals globally, bouncing EM waves over the curvature of the Earth.
  • Types:
    • LEO (Low Earth Orbit): Fast-moving, short range, low latency. Examples: Starlink, Iridium.
    • MEO (Medium Earth Orbit): GPS system satellites.
    • GEO (Geostationary Earth Orbit): Fixed position relative to Earth, used for TV, weather, and comms.

How To Receive Satellite Signals

  • Use directional antennas and tracking rotators for LEOs.
  • GEO satellites can be tracked with fixed dishes aimed at the right coordinates.
  • Be prepared for Doppler shifts and fading signals on LEOs due to rapid orbit.

Space Weather and Its Impact on Radio

  • Solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) can disrupt HF and VHF propagation.
  • Effects include scintillation, ionospheric disturbances, and blackouts.
  • Space weather alerts available via NOAA and amateur shortwave broadcasts—vital info during survival.

Atomic Clock Basics & Synchronization

  • Satellite timekeeping involves atomic clocks critical for GPS functionality.
  • Understanding clock drift and synchronization helps in timing-sensitive comm protocols.

DIY Satellite Signal Projects

  • Build a simple NOAA weather satellite signal receiver using SDR.
  • Track airplanes and satellites using ADS-B signals.
  • Receive amateur radio satellite signals for messages and telemetry.

Survival Strategy

  • Use satellite comms for long-range, decentralized emergency networks.
  • Monitor space weather to adjust radio strategies preemptively.
  • Combine satellite data and local nets for robust, layered communications.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting and Repair — Keep Your Radio Alive
chapters.html:
Introduction: When Your Radio Sucks, Your Survival Sucks

Even the best radio gear breaks down or gets outsmarted by zombies and cosmic rays. This chapter arms you with hard-won tips, tricks, and full diagnostic battle plans to keep your comms on air and zombies off your tail.

Diagnosing Common Problems

No Power / Dead Radio

  • Check batteries and power sources first.
  • Inspect fuses, switches, and connectors.
  • Use a multimeter to test volts at various circuit points.

No Sound or Faint Audio

  • Verify speaker connections.
  • Check receiver sensitivity and tuning.
  • Inspect and clean audio amplifier components.

Weak or No Transmission

  • Test antenna and cables for damage.
  • Use SWR meters to check antenna match.
  • Confirm transmitter power and modulation settings.

Noise and Interference

  • Identify sources of EMI (motors, power lines, fluorescent lighting).
  • Use ferrite beads and shielding.
  • Adjust frequency to avoid local noise bands.

Essential Tools for Radio Repair

  • Multimeter (voltage, resistance, continuity)
  • SWR meter (antenna matching)
  • Oscilloscope (waveform monitoring)
  • Signal generator (inject known signals)
  • Soldering iron and replacement parts

Step-by-Step Repair Workflow

  1. Visual inspection for obvious damage or corrosion.
  2. Power checks and voltage measurements.
  3. Signal tracing from antenna through to speaker.
  4. Component testing and replacement.
  5. Final function test on air.

Advanced Troubleshooting

  • Use spectrum analyzers or SDR to compare expected vs actual signals.
  • Monitor frequency stability and drift.
  • Diagnose microphonic and thermal noise issues.
  • Verifying digital signal sync and timing.

Zombie Survival Tip: Field Repair Kits

  • Carry a small toolkit with spare fuses, wire, connectors, and basic components.
  • Keep printouts of schematics and repair notes.
  • Practice quick field fixes under pressure.

Troubleshooting Table

Symptom Possible Cause Quick Fix
No Power Dead battery, wiring broken Replace battery, check connections
No Sound Faulty speaker, amplifier Test and swap components
Weak Signal Bad antenna, loose cable Adjust/replace antenna
Static or Noise Interference or bad ground Shield, relocate gear
Distorted Transmission Overdrive, faulty modulator Tune levels, repair circuits

chapters.title: Power & Endurance — Keep Your Radio Running While Zombies Hunt
chapters.html:
Introduction: Power Is Your Lifeblood

No power means no signal, no hack, no survival. This chapter tackles batteries, power management, alternative energy, and strategies to keep your radio gear alive when the world goes dark.

Battery Types and Selection

  • Lead Acid: Heavy, cheap, reliable. Perfect for base stations and solar banks.
  • Lithium-Ion (Li-ion): Lightweight, high energy density, but must be managed carefully.
  • Nickel-Metal Hydride (NiMH): Cheap and safer than Li-ion but lower capacity.
  • Alkaline: Great for small handheld devices, non-rechargeable, practical for spares.

Battery Care and Management

  • Avoid deep discharge to extend life.
  • Use proper chargers and charge controllers.
  • Keep batteries at moderate temperatures.
  • Monitor voltage and capacity regularly.

Solar Power Systems

  • Solar panels: Rigid or flexible, sized to your power needs.
  • Charge controllers prevent battery overcharge.
  • Batteries store solar energy for nighttime and cloudy days.
  • Portable systems useful for mobile survivors.

Power Calculation and Efficiency

  • Calculate device power draw in Watts.
  • Estimate hours of operation given battery capacity (Ah) and voltage.
  • Use power-saving modes and efficient hardware.

Alternative Power Sources

  • Hand-crank generators for emergency power.
  • Thermoelectric generators using heat differences.
  • Vehicle power taps (cigarette lighter, battery clamps).

Survival Tips

  • Carry multiple power options and recharge methods.
  • Build solar charging outposts for base stations.
  • Prep for seasonal variation — winter solar is low, have backups.

SDR Receiver 5 0.5 2.5 ~480
Handheld Transceiver 7.4 2 14.8 ~80

chapters.title: Mesh Networks and Resilient Zombieproof Data Webs
chapters.html:
Introduction: Building the Network When the Grid Is Dead

Traditional radio links can fail—zombies bite cables and fences. Mesh networks create flexible, self-healing webs for radio comms that survive attacks, jamming, and broken equipment.

What Is Mesh Networking?

  • A decentralized network of nodes (radios) where each node routes data for the others.
  • Nodes connect dynamically — if one path fails, signals reroute.
  • Increases range, resilience, and redundancy for survivors’ communications.

Key Features for Survivors

  • Self-configuring: No central server needed, just working radios.
  • Fault-tolerant: Can handle node failures or zombie destroyers.
  • Scalable: Easily add or remove nodes during survival operations.
  • Secure: Encryption and authentication options prevent hijacking.

Popular Mesh Protocols

  • 802.11s: Wi-Fi mesh standard for local networks.
  • BATMAN (Better Approach To Mobile Adhoc Networking): Optimized routing for mobile nodes.
  • OLSR (Optimized Link State Routing): Uses routing tables and proactive messaging.
  • LoRa Mesh: Long-range low power mesh for sensor networks.

Implementing Mesh in the Field

  • Use SDR or modular radios flashed with mesh-capable firmware.
  • Combine with directional antennas for long hops.
  • Experiment with open source tools: Meshtastic, cjdns, Serval Project.

Protocol Abstraction Layers in Mesh

  • Physical and link layers with frequency-agile radios.
  • Routing protocols adapting realtime topology.
  • Application layers for voice, text, or sensor data sharing.

Practical Tips

  • Start with small local meshes, expand as needed.
  • Keep spare nodes ready to replace dead radios.
  • Monitor network health and vary power to optimize battery life.

Example Mesh Use Cases

  • Emergency comms between bunkers.
  • Sharing intelligence on zombie movements.
  • Coordinating resource logistics in hostile zones.

chapters.title: Software Defined Radio (SDR) and Software Tools — Your Ultimate Radio Hack Kit
chapters.html:
Introduction: The Power of SDR

SDR turns your computer and cheap hardware into a powerful radio scanner, transmitter, and hacker’s dream device. With open-source tools, you gain unprecedented control and flexibility, essential for adaptable, zombieproof communications.

What Is SDR?

  • Unlike traditional radios with fixed hardware, SDR uses software to process signals.
  • Hardware (like RTL-SDR, HackRF, LimeSDR) digitizes incoming RF signals for software processing.
  • Output can be fully software-modulated, decoded, or analyzed.

Popular SDR Hardware

  • RTL-SDR: Ultra-cheap receiver, ideal for listening.
  • HackRF One: Full-duplex transceiver, mid-range price.
  • LimeSDR: Professional-grade SDR with wide frequency range and bandwidth.

SDR Software Tools

  • GNU Radio: Visual programming toolkit for advanced signal processing.
  • SDR# (SDRSharp): Easy-to-use Windows receiver interface.
  • GQRX: Linux/Mac GUI for SDR receivers.
  • CubicSDR: Cross-platform SDR software.
  • Python libraries: PySDR, SoapySDR for scripting and automation.

SDR Applications in Apocalypse Radio

  • Spectrum scanning and interference analysis.
  • Signal decoding (morse, pager, weather satellites).
  • Transmission and replay attacks (with legal caution).
  • Creating custom protocols and experimental modulations.

Basic SDR Setup Example (Listening)

  1. Connect RTL-SDR USB dongle.
  2. Open GQRX or SDR#.
  3. Tune FM, AM, or shortwave bands.
  4. Filter and demodulate the signals.
  5. Record or log transmissions.

Scripting & Automation

  • Python + GNU Radio flowgraphs automate signal detection.
  • Use scripts to alert you on lookout frequencies.

Introduction: The Wild World of Wave Travel

Radio doesn’t just fly straight forever—terrain, weather, and even undead hordes mess it up. This chapter explores how signals travel, bend, fade, and bounce, so you can exploit or counteract those effects.

Propagation Modes

  • Ground Wave: Follows the Earth surface; good for LF/MF bands; limited by terrain conductivity.
  • Sky Wave (Ionospheric Reflection): Bounces off ionosphere layers; enables long-range HF comms but affected by solar activity.
  • Line of Sight (LOS): Direct path, essential for VHF/UHF and microwave.
  • Tropospheric Scatter: Uses troposphere irregularities to scatter signals beyond LOS.
  • Meteor Scatter: Exploits ionized trails of meteors for brief long-distance bursts.
  • Satellite Relay: Signals bounce via orbiting satellites.

Environmental Effects on Propagation

  • Terrain: Mountains, forests, buildings absorb or reflect waves.
  • Weather: Rain, fog, and humidity can attenuate or scatter signals.
  • Temperature Inversions: Cause ducting, allowing signals to travel unusually far.
  • Solar Activity: Sunspots and solar flares cause ionospheric disturbances.
  • Urban Interference: Man-made noise worsens reception.

Wave Polarization and Its Effects

  • Orientation of the wave's electric field affects signal clarity.
  • Mismatch in polarization between TX and RX antennas causes signal loss.
  • Circular polarization useful for satellite and helicopter comms.

Fading & Multipath

  • Signal strength fluctuates due to multiple path arrivals.
  • Causes distortion, phase shift, and signal dropouts.
  • Combat with diversity antennas and spread spectrum.

Practical Propagation Tips for Survivors

  • Scout terrain and choose antenna placement with clear horizons.
  • Use higher frequencies for line-of-sight; lower for long-distance.
  • Monitor solar conditions and plan HF comms accordingly.
  • Use weather forecasts; avoid storms during critical comm windows.

Propagation Quick Formula: Free Space Path Loss (FSPL)

FSPL(dB) = 20 log10(d) + 20 log10(f) + 32.44

where d is distance in km and f frequency in MHz.

Introduction: Clean Signals Beat Zombies Every Time

Getting your radio working is one thing; getting it to stay reliable and clean through interference is another. This chapter digs into circuitry essentials for filtering noise, shaping signals, and building bulletproof radio gear.

Key Circuit Components

  • Amplifiers: Increase signal strength. Use low-noise amplifiers (LNA) near antennas.
  • Mixers: Combine signals to convert frequencies (heterodyne principle).
  • Oscillators: Generate stable carrier waves; fundamental for transmitters.
  • Filters: Remove unwanted frequencies, noise, and interference.
  • Switches & Attenuators: Control signal flow and strength.

Filters

  • Low-pass filters: Block high frequencies, allow low frequencies.
  • High-pass filters: Block low frequencies, allow higher.
  • Band-pass filters: Only allow frequencies within a set band — critical for channel purity.
  • Notch filters: Remove specific interfering frequencies.

Noise Sources & Reduction Techniques

  • Thermal noise: From resistors and semiconductors; reduce with cooling where possible.
  • Interference: Use shielding, grounding, and isolation.
  • Cross-talk: Keep signal paths separate; use twisted pair and coaxial cables.
  • Power supply noise: Use regulated, filtered power supplies.

Circuit Design Tips

  • Use proper impedance matching to maximize power transfer.
  • Keep leads short and neat to minimize parasitic capacitance and inductance.
  • Employ decoupling capacitors close to active devices.
  • Shield sensitive components and wires.

chapters.title: POCSAG, SMS, and Ringtone Formats — Decoding Basics and Protocol Insights
chapters.html:
Introduction to POCSAG

POCSAG (Post Office Code Standardisation Advisory Group) is a widely used paging protocol for sending numeric or alphanumeric messages over radio channels. It’s foundational for pager communications.

Uses 512, 1200, or 2400 baud transmission rates.

Data is encoded using a BCH (Bose–Chaudhuri–Hocquenghem) error-correcting code.

Messages include address and function bits, followed by message data.

POCSAG Decoding

Receive the bitstream via a radio or SDR tuned to the pager frequency.

Synchronize to the sync codeword to align decoding.

BCH decoding corrects bit errors.

Extract pager address and message payload.

Payload parsing differentiates numeric and alphanumeric message types.

SMS (Short Message Service) Basics

SMS uses a store-and-forward system in cellular networks.

Text messages are encoded often in 7-bit GSM default alphabet or UCS-2 for Unicode.

Messages are packetized into Protocol Data Units (PDUs) with headers including sender, recipient, timestamp.

SMS uses signaling channels in GSM, but internet-based SMS uses SMPP or other push protocols.

SMS Decoding Essentials

Decode PDU blocks to extract text and metadata.

Handle message segmentation and reassembly for long texts.

Implement character set decoding based on GSM 03.38 or UCS-2 standards.

Ringtone Formats Overview

Early mobile ringtones were simple monophonic formats, often stored in RTTTL (Ring Tone Text Transfer Language) or MIDI.

RTTTL encodes music as note, duration, and octave in plain text strings.

Modern phones use polyphonic MIDI or audio file formats (WAV, MP3).

Decoding involves interpreting note commands or parsing audio waveform data.

Practical Applications

Build a POCSAG decoder using RTL-SDR and Python libraries.

Develop SMS message interceptors for testing network security.

Write parsers for RTTTL to MIDI converters.

Use AI to classify ringtone formats and transcode between them.

Tools and Resources

chapters.title: The Zombieproof Radio Lab Essentials
chapters.html:
Welcome, fellow survivor, to the most important room in your apocalypse bunker: the radio lab. Forget the canned beans and the machetes—your real lifeline is the collection of wires, chips, and blinking LEDs that keep you connected to the outside world. In this chapter, we’ll walk through the essential tools and hardware you need to build, repair, and maintain your zombieproof radio systems. And yes, we’ll do it with a smile, because if you’re not laughing, you’re probably already a zombie.

The Radio Lab: Your Fortress of Solitude

Your radio lab is more than just a workspace; it’s your fortress of solitude, your command center, and your last line of defense against the undead. Here, you’ll find the tools that turn scraps into communication devices, and the knowledge that keeps you one step ahead of the horde.

The Essential Tools

Let’s start with the basics. Every zombieproof radio lab needs a few key tools:

Soldering Iron. The bread and butter of any electronics lab. A good soldering iron can turn a pile of scrap into a working radio. Just remember, in a zombie apocalypse, you don’t want to be the one who burns their fingers while trying to fix the last working transceiver.

Multimeter. Your multimeter is your best friend. It can tell you if a battery is dead, if a wire is broken, or if a zombie is about to break down your door (okay, maybe not that last one, but it’s close).

Oscilloscope. For the more advanced survivor, an oscilloscope can help you debug complex circuits and ensure your signals are clean and strong. It’s like having X-ray vision for your electronics.

Breadboard. The breadboard is where you prototype your circuits. It’s the playground for your ideas, where you can test out new designs without committing to soldering. Just be careful not to leave your breadboard unattended—zombies love to chew on wires.

The Hardware Arsenal

Now, let’s talk about the hardware you’ll need to build your radio systems:

Microcontrollers. Devices like the ESP32, ESP8266, and RP2040 are the brains of your radio projects. They’re cheap, powerful, and can be programmed to do just about anything. Whether you’re building a simple FM transmitter or a complex packet radio system, a microcontroller is your best bet.

chapters.title: Protocols and Security in the Apocalypse
chapters.html:
In the zombie apocalypse, communication isn’t just about sending a message—it’s about making sure that message stays secret, secure, and doesn’t get hijacked by the undead or rival survivor gangs. Radio protocols and security are your digital armor, shielding your transmissions from prying ears and malicious interference.

The Protocol Zoo

Radio protocols are the rulebooks that govern how your signals behave. From simple Morse code to complex digital packet systems, each protocol has its strengths and weaknesses. In the apocalypse, you’ll want protocols that are robust, easy to implement, and resistant to interference.

Morse Code. The granddaddy of all protocols, Morse code is simple, reliable, and can be sent with minimal equipment. It’s also hard to jam or intercept, making it perfect for emergency signals.

AX.25. This packet radio protocol is the backbone of amateur digital radio. It’s designed for noisy, unreliable channels and includes error checking and addressing, making it ideal for sending text messages or data over long distances.

UDP. For fast, connectionless communication, UDP is your go-to. It’s perfect for short bursts of data, like alerts or status updates, but lacks the reliability of more complex protocols.

Security: Keeping the Zombies Out

Security in the apocalypse isn’t just about encryption—it’s about making your communications as hard to intercept or disrupt as possible.

Encryption. Use simple ciphers or one-time pads to scramble your messages. Even basic encryption can keep your communications safe from casual eavesdroppers.

Rolling Codes. For repeated transmissions, use rolling codes that change with each message. This prevents replay attacks, where an attacker records your signal and plays it back later.

Frequency Hopping. Switch frequencies regularly to avoid jamming and eavesdropping. This technique is used in Bluetooth and some military radios, and it’s surprisingly effective against both zombies and hackers.

Practical Tips

Always use strong, unique passwords for your radios and networks.

Regularly update your protocols and security measures to stay ahead of new threats.

Keep your communications brief and to the point to minimize the risk of interception.

With the right protocols and security measures, you can keep your messages safe and your survival network thriving, even in the face of zombie hordes and digital threats.

foreword:
Someone always asks, at the bad moment, whether the radio is on. They mean: is there a voice. They mean: are we still a we.

This manual is an answer with grease on it. It begins where radio actually begins, which is not with a brand of handset but with a wave that does not care about your afternoon. Frequency, wavelength, the stubborn speed of light. Then antennas, which are only metal arranged so the air will agree with you. Then the languages signals speak when they are trying not to be mistaken for noise. Then the unglamorous trinity: power, repair, and a place to put the thing so the rain, and the neighbors, do not improve it.

You will find projects. Some of them can be done with scavenged wire and a patience you may have to borrow. Some of them want a software-defined radio, a notebook, and the humility to read the band plan before you key up. Later chapters wander into pagers, contactless scraps, packet, radar-ish tricks, and the old secret of amateur radio, which was never secret: listen more than you talk, and sign your work.

The zombies are a convenience. They stand in for every reason a network fails. Panic, distance, weather, a dead battery, a person who will not stop transmitting their grocery list on the calling frequency. If you are reading this while the world is, against the odds, still answering its phone, the zombies will not mind. The physics is the same on a Tuesday.

A word about the pages that mention jamming, interception, and cleverness at other people’s expense. Cleverness is not a license. The book says so in its own chapters, and the copyright page says so again, because some readers skip to the interesting part. Be one of the ones who does not.

What I hope you keep is not a single circuit. It is the habit of a net: a time, a frequency, a way to say you are still there, and a way to say it shorter than your fear would prefer. Radios are poor company and excellent neighbors. They do not replace the person on the other end. They only make it possible for that person to be far away and still count.

Leave your name off the title page until you want it there. The air does not require a byline. It requires a carrier, a little discipline, and somebody listening at the hour you promised.
preface:
This manual was assembled from a stack of chapter drafts. They did not all arrive in the same handwriting. The early chapters are tight, technical, and fond of a formula. The later ones are looser, more of a campfire brief, and once or twice they promise a code listing that was never in the pile. Where a draft pointed at a missing file, or told you to see “the next markdown,” that crumb has been swept off the bench. The chapters themselves are the ones you brought.

You can read it straight through, or raid the contents the way you would raid a parts bin. Part I is the physics you will pretend you already knew. The middle is wire, power, weather, and repair. The last third is protocols, lab scraps, and the long business of staying hearable.

The formulas are the ordinary ones. An antenna in a real wind will disagree with them a little. That is not the formula being rude.

There is a dull warning, and it is dull on purpose. Do not jam a frequency you do not have the right to touch. Do not intercept what is not yours. Do not transmit where you are not allowed. The jokes are jokes. A grid can fail and the rules about the spectrum can still be standing. Mains voltage does not care that you are improvising. If a chapter invites you to open a thing that plugs into a wall, assume it can bite.

The dedication, the author’s name, and the publisher are blank on purpose. Write them in when you know them. Ink, not pencil. Pencil is for frequencies.
afterword:
The last chapter of a radio book is a temptation to get solemn. Resist it a little. The band is not a chapel. It is a bench you share with strangers, and the courtesy that keeps it usable is older than any of us: listen first, sign your work, leave a gap so someone else can answer.

If you have read this far you already know the unglamorous truth. Range is an antenna and a clear path more often than it is a bigger battery. A net is a promise about time as much as it is a piece of hardware. Encryption is a tool, not a personality. And the person who brings a spare connector will be remembered more kindly than the person who brings a speech.

The zombies, if you still need them, are only the name we gave the interruption. Weather is one. A dead coax is one. Panic on the calling frequency is one. You do not beat them by being louder. You beat them by being findable, brief, and still there at the hour you named.

Leave a frequency in the log. Tell someone else what it is. When you are done for the night, say so, and mean it, so nobody sits up listening to static out of loyalty.

The signature under an afterword belongs to the person who stands by the book. That line is blank until you want it.

73 — which is to say, best regards — and then quiet.
